section.title: Theme B: Religion and life
section.blurb: Origins of the universe and life, caring for the world and animals, abortion, euthanasia and life after death, from Christian, Jewish and non-religious points of view.

topics.title: The origins of the universe
topics.overview: Christians and Jews believe God created the universe, while science explains its development with the Big Bang. You need religious creation teachings, different ways of interpreting them, and how believers relate them to science.

bullets: Christians and Jews believe God created the universe. Genesis 1 describes creation in six days, with God resting on the seventh. Many believe God created 'out of nothing' (**creation ex nihilo**), simply by his word: 'And God said, Let there be light, and there was light' (Genesis 1:3).

Genesis 2 gives a second account, focused on the creation of Adam and Eve in the Garden of Eden. Many scholars see the two accounts as teaching truths about God rather than a single scientific record.
Christians add that everything was made through the Word, Jesus (John 1:1-3), and that God's Spirit was present (Genesis 1:2), so the whole Trinity was involved in creation.

Creation teaches that God is all-powerful (omnipotent), that the world is 'very good' (Genesis 1:31) and has a purpose, and that it belongs to God. Jews traditionally count years from creation: autumn 2026 began the Jewish year 5787.

The **Big Bang theory** says the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago from an extremely hot, dense point (a singularity), then expanded and cooled, forming atoms, stars and galaxies. It is still expanding.

Evidence includes the galaxies moving away from each other (red shift, shown by Edwin Hubble in 1929) and cosmic microwave background radiation, the 'afterglow' of the Big Bang (discovered 1964 to 1965).

The theory was first proposed in 1927 by Georges Lemaitre, a Belgian Catholic priest and physicist. Science explains how the universe developed, but many say it cannot explain why there is something rather than nothing.

notes.h: Different interpretations and the relationship with science
bullets: **Creationists** (some Evangelical Christians and some Orthodox Jews) read Genesis literally as God's word: God made everything in six 24-hour days, and many 'Young Earth' creationists believe the earth is only thousands of years old. They reject or reinterpret the Big Bang.
Some read the 'days' as long ages (each 'day' an era), so Genesis and science follow a similar order.

Most Christians and many Jews read Genesis as a symbolic or poetic story that teaches why the world exists (God made it with love and purpose), while science explains how. The Catholic Church accepts the Big Bang; Pope Francis said in 2014 that God is 'not a magician' and that the Big Bang does not contradict creation but needs it. Rabbi Jonathan Sacks wrote that science takes things apart to see how they work, while religion puts things together to see what they mean.
Some believers say the Big Bang supports God: something must have caused it (the First Cause argument), and the finely tuned laws of physics suggest a designer.

**Atheists and humanists** say the universe can be explained by natural laws and the Big Bang, with no need for God (for example Stephen Hawking argued this). Creation stories are seen as myths from a time before science.

views.label: Orthodox Jewish
views.text: The Torah is God's word and God created the world. Some read the six days literally; others read them as long periods and accept the Big Bang.

views.label: Reform and Liberal Jewish
views.text: Genesis is an inspired, symbolic story. God is the creator and science explains the process.

views.label: Atheist and humanist
views.text: The Big Bang and natural laws explain the universe without any need for God, and religious creation accounts are myths.

topics.title: The value of the world and the duty to protect it
topics.overview: Christians and Jews believe the world is valuable because God made it, and this gives humans a duty to look after it. The key ideas named in the specification are stewardship, dominion, responsibility, and awe and wonder.

bullets: Christians and Jews believe God created the world and it still belongs to him: 'The earth is the Lord's, and everything in it' (Psalm 24:1). Humans do not own it; they are trusted with it.
God saw that creation was 'very good' (Genesis 1:31), so it has value in itself, not just because it is useful to humans.

**Awe and wonder** is the feeling of amazement and respect at the beauty and scale of nature, such as mountains, oceans and the night sky. Many believers see God revealed in it: 'The heavens declare the glory of God' (Psalm 19:1), and Paul says God's power can be seen in what he made (Romans 1:20). Non-religious people also feel awe at nature, but explain it through science.
The world is also valuable because all life, including future generations, depends on it.

**Stewardship** is the idea that believers have a duty from God to look after the world. God put Adam in Eden 'to work it and take care of it' (Genesis 2:15). A steward looks after something for its owner and will have to account for it, as in the Parable of the Talents (Matthew 25:14-30).

**Dominion** means dominance, power or control. God told humans to 'rule over' the fish, birds and animals (Genesis 1:26-28). In the past some used this to justify exploiting nature. Today most Christians and Jews say it means ruling like a good king: responsible, caring power, because humans are made in God's image.

**Responsibility** means having a duty to care for, or having control over, someone or something. Believers are responsible to God, to other people (especially the poor, who suffer most from environmental damage), and to future generations.

Jewish teachings: **Tikkun Olam** ('repairing the world'); **bal tashchit** ('do not destroy', based on Deuteronomy 20:19-20); the **Shmita** year, when the land rests every seventh year (Leviticus 25:4); and Tu BiShvat, the new year for trees. A Jewish story (Midrash Kohelet Rabbah 7:13) has God tell Adam, 'Do not ruin and destroy my world, for if you do, there is no one to repair it after you.'

Believers show stewardship by recycling, saving energy, cutting car journeys, planting trees and choosing ethical products. Churches join A Rocha UK's **Eco Church** scheme; the Church of England set a target of net zero carbon by 2030; Jewish communities run EcoJudaism projects.
Pope Francis wrote **Laudato Si'** (2015), on 'care for our common home', and Laudate Deum (2023), urging action on climate change.

**Non-religious views**: humanists say we have a duty to protect the world because it is the only home humans and other life have, and because future generations deserve a healthy planet. This duty comes from reason and compassion, not God.

views.label: Humanist

topics.title: The use and abuse of the environment
topics.overview: The environment gives humans natural resources, but misuse damages it. Christians and Jews teach that stewardship means using resources carefully and fairly, for the poor and for future generations.

bullets: **Natural resources** are materials found in nature that can be used by living things, such as oil, coal, gas, water, trees, soil and minerals. Some are **non-renewable** (fossil fuels will run out) and some are **renewable** (wind, solar, wave power).

Abuse of the environment includes deforestation (for example in the Amazon), over-fishing, wasting water, using up fossil fuels and producing greenhouse gases that cause **climate change**: hotter summers, floods, droughts and rising seas.
Causes include a growing world population (over 8 billion), rising consumption in richer countries and a 'throwaway' culture.

**Sustainable development** means meeting today's needs without damaging the ability of future generations to meet theirs. The Paris Agreement (2015) aims to limit global warming to well below 2 degrees Celsius; the UK has a legal target of net zero emissions by 2050.

Christians and Jews teach the earth belongs to God (Psalm 24:1) and humans are like tenants: 'the land is mine and you reside in my land as foreigners and strangers' (Leviticus 25:23). So humans must use resources carefully and not waste them.
The Parable of the Talents (Matthew 25:14-30) teaches that God will judge how humans have used what he trusted to them.
Abusing the environment hurts the poor most, so it breaks Jesus' command to love your neighbour (Matthew 22:39) and to care for 'the least of these' (Matthew 25:40).

Pope Francis's Laudato Si' (2015) says the climate is 'a common good' and calls for 'ecological conversion'. St Francis of Assisi is the patron saint of ecology. In 1986 leaders of world faiths met at Assisi and made declarations on caring for nature.
Jewish teaching: bal tashchit (Deuteronomy 20:19-20) forbids needless destruction; Tikkun Olam calls Jews to repair the world; the Shmita year lets the land rest.

Believers can recycle, save energy and water, travel less by car or plane, plant trees, buy local, fair-trade and sustainable goods, and join or support groups such as Eco Church, A Rocha, CAFOD, Christian Aid, Tearfund and EcoJudaism.

**Non-religious views**: humanists and atheists support protecting the environment for human survival and wellbeing and for other species, based on scientific evidence. A utilitarian would say damaging the environment causes huge suffering for the greatest number, now and in future.

views.label: Christian stewardship
views.text: Humans are caretakers of God's creation, so abusing it is a sin against God, the poor and future generations. Believers should live simply and campaign for change.

views.label: Jewish

views.label: Humanist
views.text: Environmental protection is needed for human survival, the welfare of other species and future generations, based on science and reason.

topics.title: Pollution
topics.overview: Pollution damages God's creation and harms people, animals and plants. Religious believers use stewardship and love of neighbour to argue that pollution is wrong, and take practical action to reduce it.

bullets: **Pollution** is making something dirty and contaminated, especially the environment.

**Air pollution**: fumes from vehicles, power stations and factories. It causes asthma and lung disease (linked to tens of thousands of early deaths a year in the UK) and greenhouse gases add to climate change.

**Water pollution**: oil spills (for example Deepwater Horizon, 2010), sewage, factory chemicals and farm fertilisers. Sewage discharges into UK rivers and seas have been a major news issue in the 2020s.
**Land pollution**: rubbish and landfill, toxic waste and pesticides. **Plastic pollution** affects land and sea: plastic breaks into microplastics that enter food chains.
Other types include noise and light pollution, and radioactive waste.
Pollution goes against **stewardship**: the world is on loan from God (Psalm 24:1, Genesis 2:15) and should be handed on in good condition.
Pollution harms other people, especially the poor and future generations, which goes against 'love your neighbour as yourself' (Matthew 22:39).
Pope Francis in Laudato Si' (2015) warned that the earth is beginning to look like 'an immense pile of filth' and criticised a 'throwaway culture'.

Jewish teaching: bal tashchit forbids needless destruction; Tikkun Olam calls Jews to repair the world; and the Torah's laws about keeping the camp clean (Deuteronomy 23:12-13) show care for the shared environment.
Personal: use public transport, walk or cycle, cut single-use plastic, recycle and reuse, save energy, pick up litter.

Community and political: churches and synagogues install solar panels, join Eco Church, hold litter picks, and campaign through Christian Aid, Tearfund, CAFOD and Operation Noah. Governments make laws and treaties, such as the UK Climate Change Act 2008, the 5p plastic bag charge (2015, now 10p) and the Paris Agreement (2015).

**Non-religious views**: humanists support reducing pollution to protect human health and other species, using scientific evidence; a utilitarian focuses on the harm pollution does to the greatest number.

views.label: Christian
views.text: Pollution is a failure of stewardship and harms the neighbours God asks us to love. Believers should reduce their own pollution and campaign for change.

views.label: Jewish
views.text: Pollution damages God's world and breaks bal tashchit. Jews are called to repair the world through Tikkun Olam.

views.label: Humanist
views.text: Pollution harms health and ecosystems, and should be reduced to protect people, other species and future generations, based on scientific evidence.

topics.title: The use and abuse of animals
topics.overview: Christians and Jews believe animals are God's creatures and must be treated kindly, but most also believe humans matter more. Animal experimentation is one of the three Theme B issues where you must explain contrasting beliefs. You also need the use of animals for food.

bullets: God created animals and saw that they were good (Genesis 1:25). Jesus said not one sparrow is forgotten by God (Luke 12:6), and 'the righteous care for the needs of their animals' (Proverbs 12:10). The Sabbath rest includes animals (Exodus 23:12).

Humans are made in God's image and given dominion (Genesis 1:26), so most Christians and Jews believe human life is of greater value and humans may use animals, but never cruelly. The Catholic Catechism says animals are God's creatures and it is wrong to cause them to suffer or die needlessly (CCC 2418).

Jewish law forbids causing unnecessary pain to animals (**tza'ar ba'alei chayim**). Examples: 'Do not muzzle an ox while it is treading out the grain' (Deuteronomy 25:4), and animals must be fed before their owners eat.
The RSPCA was founded in 1824 by a group including an Anglican priest, Arthur Broome. UK law: the Animal Welfare Act 2006 makes cruelty and neglect illegal.

**Animal experimentation** means performing scientific tests on animals, usually to develop medicines or check the safety of products. In Great Britain it is controlled by the Animals (Scientific Procedures) Act 1986: researchers need licences and must follow the **3Rs**: replace animals where possible, reduce the numbers used, refine methods to reduce suffering.

Testing cosmetics and their ingredients on animals has been banned in the UK since 1998. In 2025 there were about 2.54 million procedures in Great Britain, the lowest since the 1986 Act, mostly on mice (Home Office). In November 2025 the government published a strategy to speed up replacing animals in science.

**For (Catholic Church and many Christians)**: 'Medical and scientific experimentation on animals is a morally acceptable practice if it remains within reasonable limits and contributes to caring for or saving human lives' (CCC 2417). Humans are made in God's image, so saving human life justifies it, if suffering is minimised. Many medicines and vaccines were developed with animal research.

**For (Judaism)**: Orthodox Judaism generally allows experiments that are genuinely needed to save human life (pikuach nefesh), as humans may use animals for their needs, provided pain is kept to a minimum (tza'ar ba'alei chayim).

**Against (some Christians, especially those concerned with animal welfare)**: animals have value to God, so causing them suffering for human benefit is cruel and abuses dominion. The Anglican theologian Andrew Linzey argues animals have God-given rights. Alternatives such as computer models and lab-grown cells now exist.

**Non-religious views**: some atheists and humanists support research that is necessary for medicine with strict welfare rules. Others, such as the philosopher Peter Singer, say favouring humans just because they are human is 'speciesism' and that the suffering of animals counts equally. Animal rights groups argue animal results do not always apply to humans.

notes.h: The use of animals for food
bullets: Genesis 1:29 gives humans plants to eat, but after the flood God says 'Everything that lives and moves about will be food for you' (Genesis 9:3). Most Christians eat meat; Peter's vision (Acts 10) is often used to show all foods are allowed. Some Christians, for example many Seventh-day Adventists, are vegetarian out of concern for health and animals.

Jews may eat meat only if it is **kosher**: from permitted animals (no pork or shellfish), killed by **shechita** (a single quick cut by a trained shochet to minimise pain), with the blood removed, and never mixed with milk. Hunting for sport is discouraged.

Concerns for many believers and non-believers: factory farming, which crowds animals and limits natural behaviour; environmental damage from meat production. Many choose free-range, organic, vegetarian or vegan diets. Humanists generally judge by the amount of suffering caused.

views.label: Orthodox Jewish

views.label: Humanist

topics.title: The origins of human life
topics.overview: Christians and Jews believe God made humans in his image, while science explains human origins through evolution. You need religious teachings, different interpretations of them, and how believers relate them to evolution.

bullets: Genesis 1 says God created humans on the sixth day, 'in his own image... male and female' (Genesis 1:27), and gave them responsibility for the rest of creation.

Genesis 2 says God formed Adam from the dust of the ground and 'breathed into his nostrils the breath of life' (Genesis 2:7), then made Eve from Adam's rib. The breath of God is often understood as the soul.

Humans are special because they are made in the **image of God** (imago Dei): they can think, love, make moral choices and have a relationship with God. Christians and Jews believe this gives every human life a unique value (the basis of the sanctity of life).

**Evolution** is the scientific theory that living things have developed over millions of years from simpler forms. The process is **natural selection**: living things with features that help them survive in their environment are more likely to reproduce and pass those features on. Charles Darwin set this out in On the Origin of Species (1859).
Evidence includes fossils, similarities in anatomy, and DNA, which shows humans share common ancestors with apes. Modern humans (Homo sapiens) appeared in Africa roughly 300,000 years ago.
Evolution suggests humans developed gradually rather than being made separately, which seems to conflict with a literal reading of Genesis.

**Creationists** (some Evangelical Christians and some Orthodox Jews) take Genesis literally and reject evolution, especially for humans. Some support **intelligent design**: the idea that living things are too complex to have developed by chance, so a designer must be responsible.

**Theistic evolution**: most Christians and many Jews accept evolution as God's way of creating life. Genesis is a symbolic story explaining why humans exist and that they are special to God; science explains how.

The **Catholic Church** allows belief in evolution of the body (Pope Pius XII, 1950), and Pope John Paul II said in 1996 that evolution is 'more than a hypothesis'. But it teaches that each human soul is created directly by God.

**Atheists and humanists** accept evolution as a complete natural explanation, with no need for God; Richard Dawkins argues natural selection explains the appearance of design. Humanists still value human life highly, because of what humans can think, feel and achieve.

views.label: Catholic

views.label: Orthodox Jewish
views.text: God created humans, as the Torah teaches. Some reject evolution; others accept it as the method God used.

views.label: Reform and Liberal Jewish
views.text: Genesis is symbolic, and evolution is God's way of bringing about life. Its message is that every human is made in God's image.

views.label: Atheist and humanist
views.text: Evolution by natural selection fully explains how humans developed, so no creator is needed. Human value comes from human abilities and relationships.

topics.title: The sanctity of life and the quality of life
topics.overview: The sanctity of life (life is sacred) and the quality of life (how good a life is) are the two key concepts behind abortion and euthanasia. The specification names arguments based on both.

bullets: **Sanctity of life** is the belief that all life is holy because it is created by God and belongs to him. Humans are made in God's image (Genesis 1:27) and receive the breath of life from God (Genesis 2:7).

Because life is God's gift, only God has the right to end it: 'The Lord gave and the Lord has taken away' (Job 1:21). 'You shall not murder' (Exodus 20:13). Paul says 'your bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit... You are not your own' (1 Corinthians 6:19-20).

Catholics teach that every human life is sacred from conception to natural death, whatever its condition. Judaism teaches that one life has infinite value: whoever saves a single life is as if they saved an entire world (Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5). The principle of **pikuach nefesh** means saving life overrides almost all other commandments, such as Shabbat rules.
Some non-religious people also hold a non-religious version: human life is special and should be protected, even if they do not believe it is God-given.
**Quality of life** is the general wellbeing of a person, in relation to their health and happiness; also the theory that the value of life depends on how good or how satisfying it is.

Supporters say that if a life is full of severe pain and suffering with no hope of improvement, ending it, or not starting it, may be the most loving choice. Doctors also use quality of life when deciding whether treatment is worth giving.

**Situation ethics** (Joseph Fletcher, 1966) says Christians should do the most loving thing (agape) in each situation rather than follow fixed rules, so quality of life can matter more than a rule against killing. A **utilitarian** (principle of utility: the greatest good for the greatest number) weighs the happiness and suffering of everyone affected. The philosopher Peter Singer argues the value of a life depends on its quality and the person's interests.
Strict sanctity of life: life must never be deliberately ended, whatever its quality. Catholics and Orthodox Jews mostly hold this, while still allowing pain relief and stopping burdensome treatment.

Weighted view: life is sacred, but compassion and quality of life can sometimes justify exceptions, for example abortion to save a mother, or allowing a dying person to refuse treatment. Many Protestants and Reform Jews hold this.
Critics of the quality of life view worry it could suggest some lives, such as those of disabled people, are worth less. Critics of strict sanctity say it can force people to suffer.

views.label: Catholic
views.text: Life is a gift from God, sacred from conception to natural death. Its value does not depend on its quality, so deliberately ending innocent life is always wrong.

views.label: Liberal Christian
views.text: Life is sacred, but compassion and quality of life can sometimes be weighed against it, especially to prevent great suffering. Love (agape) should guide each case.

views.label: Orthodox Jewish
views.text: Every life has infinite value and saving life overrides almost every other law (pikuach nefesh). Life may not be actively shortened, even when its quality is poor.

views.label: Humanist
views.text: Human life is valuable because of what people can experience and do, not because God gave it. Quality of life and a person's own wishes matter greatly.

topics.tip: Define both terms and show how they can clash. Most 12-mark answers on abortion and euthanasia turn on sanctity of life versus quality of life.
pitfalls: Do not mix up the two terms: 'quality of life' is about how good a life is, 'sanctity of life' is about life being holy (a common wrong answer in multiple-choice questions).
Do not say only religious people value life: many humanists do too, for different reasons.
The Christian sanctity of life is about human life; do not use it as a reason against animal experiments.

topics.title: Abortion
topics.overview: Abortion is one of the three Theme B issues where you must explain contrasting beliefs. You need the law (as of 2026), situations where the mother's life is at risk, Christian (Catholic and Protestant), Jewish and non-religious views, and ethical arguments based on the sanctity of life and quality of life.

notes.h: What it is and the law (as of November 2026)
bullets: **Abortion** is the removal of a foetus from the womb before it can survive, done deliberately to end a pregnancy. A **miscarriage** is when this happens naturally.

**Abortion Act 1967** (England, Wales and Scotland): abortion is legal up to 24 weeks (the limit was 28 weeks until 1990) if two doctors agree that continuing the pregnancy would risk the physical or mental health of the woman or her existing children more than ending it. There is no time limit if the woman's life is at risk, there is a risk of grave permanent injury to her, or there is a substantial risk the baby would be born with a serious disability.

Since 2022 women in England and Wales can take early medical abortion pills at home up to 10 weeks after a remote consultation. Since October 2024 'safe access zones' (150 metres) stop protests and influencing people outside clinics.

**Crime and Policing Act 2026** (Royal Assent April 2026): a woman can no longer be prosecuted for ending her own pregnancy in England and Wales, at any stage, and past convictions are pardoned. The Abortion Act rules for doctors are unchanged, and anyone else who ends a pregnancy outside the law can still be prosecuted. Supporters said women in crisis need care, not prison; opponents, including Catholic bishops and pro-life groups, said it removes protection for late pregnancies.

In Northern Ireland abortion has been legal on request up to 12 weeks since 2020. In 2023 there were about 278,000 abortions for residents of England and Wales; 87% were medical (pill) abortions and 89% took place under 10 weeks (DHSC; later figures were delayed).

Views include: at **conception** (Catholic teaching); when the heart begins to beat or the brain develops; at **viability**, when the foetus could survive outside the womb (around 24 weeks, the basis of UK law); or at birth (traditional Jewish teaching that the foetus becomes a full person when its head or most of its body has emerged).

**Pro-life** groups (such as SPUC and Right to Life UK) argue the unborn child has a right to life from conception. **Pro-choice** groups (such as BPAS and Humanists UK) argue a woman has the right to decide what happens to her own body.

**Catholic Church**: human life must be respected and protected absolutely from the moment of conception (Catechism 2270), so direct abortion is always gravely wrong, even after rape or with a disability. Sources: Jeremiah 1:5, Psalm 139:13, Exodus 20:13. The Church supports women through pregnancy and adoption. **Mother's life at risk**: by the principle of **double effect**, treatment to save the mother (for example removing a cancerous womb or an ectopic pregnancy) is allowed even if the foetus dies, because its death is foreseen but not intended.

**Church of England**: strongly opposes abortion as a form of birth control and sees the foetus as a human life to be protected, but accepts that in strictly limited cases, such as a serious risk to the mother's life or health, abortion may be morally preferable to any other option (the lesser of two evils).

**Methodists and many liberal Protestants**: life is sacred, but each situation is different; abortion can sometimes be the lesser evil, and the decision should be made responsibly, with care and support for the woman. They stress compassion (Matthew 5:7) and the 'most loving thing' (situation ethics).
**Evangelical Christians**: most are strongly pro-life, for the same reasons as Catholics, though many accept abortion to save the mother's life.

Life is sacred, but the foetus is not yet a full person: in Exodus 21:22 causing a miscarriage is punished by a fine, not as murder. The Talmud describes the embryo in the first 40 days as 'mere water'.

**Mother's life at risk**: abortion is required, because 'her life comes before its life' (Mishnah Oholot 7:6). Once most of the baby is born, it cannot be harmed, as one life cannot be set aside for another.

**Orthodox Judaism**: abortion only for serious reasons, mainly danger to the mother's life or health (some rabbis include serious mental health risk), after consulting a rabbi. **Reform Judaism**: the woman decides, after careful thought, and Reform Jews support legal access to abortion.

notes.h: Ethical arguments: sanctity of life versus quality of life
bullets: **Sanctity of life** argument (against): the foetus is a human life made by God, so ending it is wrong whatever the circumstances; even a disabled child's life is equally sacred.

**Quality of life** argument (for, in some cases): the quality of life of the mother (health, age, rape, poverty) and of the child (severe abnormality) should be considered; bringing a child into great suffering may not be loving.

**Utilitarian** argument: consider the happiness and suffering of everyone affected: the woman, the child, the family. **Humanists** usually support a woman's right to choose, believing a foetus is not yet a person with interests in early pregnancy, while taking the decision seriously.
Some non-religious people are pro-life, for example on the grounds that the foetus is a potential human with a right to life, or concern about abortions because of disability.

views.label: Catholic
views.text: Life begins at conception, so direct abortion is always wrong, even after rape. Treatment to save the mother's life is allowed if the death of the foetus is not intended (double effect).

views.label: Church of England
views.text: Abortion is a serious matter and the unborn child has value, but it may be the lesser of two evils in strictly limited circumstances, such as a serious risk to the mother.

views.label: Methodist and liberal Protestant
views.text: Life is sacred, but each situation is different and the woman's wellbeing matters. Abortion can sometimes be the lesser evil, decided responsibly and with compassion.

views.label: Orthodox Jewish
views.text: The foetus is precious but not a full person until birth. Abortion is required if the mother's life is at risk and allowed for serious threats to her health, but not for convenience.

views.label: Reform Jewish
views.text: The woman should decide after careful thought, including for her mental health or the family's welfare, and abortion should be legally available.

views.label: Humanist
views.text: A woman has the right to decide about her own body. An early foetus is not yet a person, so quality of life and the woman's wellbeing carry great weight.

views.label: Non-religious pro-life
views.text: Without relying on God, the unborn child is a developing human being with a right to life, and abortion harms the child and sometimes the mother.

pitfalls: Do not quote the law as if it were religious teaching. Say what the law allows, then what a religion teaches about it.
Read the statement carefully: 'Religious believers should be against abortion' asks about believers, not whether abortion is right in general.
Do not say 'all Christians are against abortion'. Contrast Catholic teaching with the Church of England or Methodists.

topics.title: Euthanasia
topics.overview: Euthanasia is one of the three Theme B issues where you must explain contrasting beliefs. You need the types, the UK law as of 2026 (including the failed assisted dying bills), and Christian, Jewish and non-religious views.

bullets: **Euthanasia** means the painless killing of a patient suffering from an incurable disease or an irreversible coma (from Greek words meaning 'good death').

**Voluntary** euthanasia: at the patient's own request. **Non-voluntary**: the patient cannot ask (for example in a coma) and others decide. **Involuntary**: against the patient's wishes, which is murder.

**Active** euthanasia: deliberately doing something to end life, such as a lethal injection. **Passive** euthanasia: withdrawing or withholding treatment that keeps someone alive, so they die of their illness. **Assisted suicide** (assisted dying): helping a person to end their own life, for example by supplying lethal drugs.

Euthanasia and assisted suicide are illegal throughout the UK. The Suicide Act 1961 stopped suicide being a crime, but helping someone to die can bring up to 14 years in prison. Since 2010 prosecutors' guidance says a person acting only out of compassion, at the clear request of the person who died, is less likely to be prosecuted.
Patients can refuse treatment, doctors can stop treatment that is not in a patient's best interests, and doctors can give pain relief even if it might shorten life (double effect). These are legal.

The **Terminally Ill Adults (End of Life) Bill**, for adults in England and Wales with six months or less to live, passed the House of Commons in June 2025 (314 to 291) but ran out of time in the House of Lords in April 2026. A new version was **defeated** in the Commons on 11 September 2026 (286 to 270). In March 2026 the Scottish Parliament also voted down an assisted dying bill. The debate is likely to continue.
Some other countries allow forms of it, for example Switzerland (assisted suicide, including the Dignitas clinic), the Netherlands, Belgium, Canada and several US and Australian states.

**Catholic Church**: euthanasia is 'morally unacceptable' because it deliberately kills a human being (Catechism 2277). Life is God's gift, sacred until natural death. But it is acceptable to stop 'burdensome, dangerous, extraordinary' treatment that only prolongs dying (Catechism 2278), and to give strong painkillers (double effect).

**Church of England**: opposes changing the law, saying it would put pressure on vulnerable, elderly and disabled people to feel a burden. It supports palliative care and hospices. Leaders of many faiths opposed the 2025 to 2026 bills.

**Hospices** give **palliative care**: relief from pain and symptoms, and emotional and spiritual support, to help people die with dignity. The modern hospice movement began with Dame Cicely Saunders, a Christian nurse and doctor, who opened St Christopher's Hospice in London in 1967.

**Some Christians support assisted dying**: they argue that Jesus showed compassion to the suffering ('Blessed are the merciful', Matthew 5:7) and that love (agape, situation ethics) can mean ending unbearable pain. Former Archbishop of Canterbury Lord Carey and Archbishop Desmond Tutu both spoke in favour.

**Orthodox Judaism**: life belongs to God and each moment of life is precious, so active euthanasia is forbidden and counts as murder. However, it is allowed to remove something that only delays the death of someone who is actively dying. Pikuach nefesh means doctors must try to save life.
**Reform Judaism**: more open. Some Reform rabbis, such as Rabbi Jonathan Romain, campaign for assisted dying with safeguards, arguing compassion and the person's choice matter.

**Humanists** (Humanists UK) support legal assisted dying for people who are terminally ill or incurably suffering and mentally competent, with safeguards: people should have autonomy over their own lives and a right to a dignified death. A utilitarian may argue it reduces suffering overall.

**Non-religious opponents** (including many doctors and disability rights groups) worry about pressure on vulnerable people, mistakes in diagnosis, a 'slippery slope' to non-voluntary euthanasia, and damage to trust in doctors.

views.label: Catholic
views.text: Euthanasia is always wrong because life is sacred until natural death. Pain should be relieved through palliative care, and burdensome treatment may be stopped, but life must not be deliberately ended.

views.label: Church of England
views.text: Assisted dying should not be legalised because it would put pressure on vulnerable people. Hospices and good palliative care are the right response.

views.label: Liberal Christian
views.text: Compassion may justify helping a dying person who clearly asks to end unbearable suffering. Love and mercy are central to Jesus' teaching.

views.label: Orthodox Jewish
views.text: Active euthanasia is forbidden as murder, but treatment that only delays the death of someone actively dying need not be continued.

views.label: Reform Jewish
views.text: More willing to accept a person's choice of a dignified death in some cases, with strong safeguards.

views.label: Humanist
views.text: Mentally competent adults who are terminally ill or incurably suffering should have the legal right to an assisted death, with safeguards.

views.label: Non-religious opponent
views.text: Even without belief in God, legalising it is too dangerous: vulnerable people could feel pressured, diagnoses can be wrong, and trust in doctors could suffer.

topics.title: Death and the afterlife
topics.overview: Christians and Jews believe death is not the end, and this affects how they live and how they value human life. You also need non-religious views and arguments for and against belief in life after death.

bullets: Christians believe in life after death because Jesus rose from the dead and promised eternal life: 'I am the resurrection and the life' (John 11:25). Most believe the soul lives on, and many believe in the **resurrection** of the body in a new, glorified, spiritual form (1 Corinthians 15:42-44).

God will **judge** each person. In the Parable of the Sheep and the Goats (Matthew 25:31-46) people are judged on how they treated those in need. **Heaven** is eternal life with God, without death or pain (Revelation 21:4); **hell** is separation from God.

**Catholics** also believe in **purgatory**, where souls are cleansed before heaven, and pray for the dead. **Protestants** stress that salvation comes through faith and God's grace, and most reject purgatory. Some Christians believe all will eventually be saved, or that hell is not eternal torment.
Jewish teaching on the afterlife is less detailed, because the focus is on living by God's mitzvot now. Many Jews believe in **Olam Ha-Ba** (the world to come).

**Orthodox Judaism**: God will raise the dead in the Messianic age ('Multitudes who sleep in the dust of the earth will awake', Daniel 12:2; one of Maimonides' 13 principles). So the body is buried quickly and cremation is avoided. The soul may be purified in Gehinnom for up to twelve months, which is why mourners say Kaddish for eleven months.
**Reform and Liberal Judaism**: many believe the soul lives on with God rather than in bodily resurrection; some are unsure, and cremation is accepted.

notes.h: Impact on beliefs about the value of human life
bullets: Because this life leads to eternity and judgement, Christians and Jews see it as precious and accountable: it should be used to love God and help others, not wasted or ended early. This supports the sanctity of life and opposition to murder, suicide and euthanasia.
Belief in heaven gives comfort and hope to the dying and the bereaved, so death need not be feared, and believers may accept death peacefully rather than seek to end life.

**Atheists and humanists** believe death is the end of the person. They argue this makes life more valuable, because it is the only one we have: we should make the most of it, be happy and help others now. People live on through their children, achievements and others' memories. Humanist funerals celebrate the life lived.

notes.h: Arguments for and against life after death
bullets: **For**: the resurrection of Jesus and the teachings of scripture; religious experiences; near-death experiences, where people report leaving their body or seeing a light; claims of mediums or memories of past lives; the idea that the mind or soul is different from the brain; the belief that a just God must reward good and punish evil.

**Against**: there is no scientific evidence; the mind seems to depend on the brain, so when the brain dies so does the person; near-death experiences can be explained by lack of oxygen or drugs; belief may be wishful thinking to cope with fear of death (Freud); different religions describe the afterlife in very different ways.

views.label: Catholic
views.text: The soul is immortal. After death comes judgement, then heaven, hell or purgatory, and the body will be raised at the end of time. Prayer for the dead is valuable.

views.label: Protestant
views.text: Life continues after death, with judgement and heaven or hell. Salvation comes through faith in Jesus and God's grace. Purgatory is not accepted.

views.label: Orthodox Jewish
views.text: The soul survives and the dead will be raised in the Messianic age, so the body must be buried, not cremated. Everyone is accountable to God, so life should be lived by the mitzvot.

views.label: Reform and Liberal Jewish
views.text: Many focus on the soul living on with God rather than bodily resurrection, accept cremation, and put the emphasis on this life.

views.label: Atheist and humanist
views.text: Death is the end of the person. Life is precious because it is the only one we have, and people live on through their influence and others' memories.

flashcards.q: What is the Big Bang theory?
flashcards.a: The scientific theory that the universe began about 13.8 billion years ago from a tiny, hot, dense point (a singularity), then expanded and cooled to form stars and galaxies.

flashcards.q: What does creation ex nihilo mean?
flashcards.a: Creation out of nothing. Many Christians and Jews believe God made the universe from nothing, simply by his word.

flashcards.q: What does Genesis 1:3 teach about God?
flashcards.a: God said 'Let there be light', and there was light. It shows God is all-powerful and can create just by speaking.

flashcards.q: Why do some Christians reject the Big Bang?
flashcards.a: They take Genesis literally as God's word, so believe he made the world in six days, and see the Bible as more reliable than science.

flashcards.q: How can a Christian accept both the Big Bang and creation?
flashcards.a: They can say Genesis is symbolic, that the Big Bang was God's method, and that science explains how while religion explains why.

flashcards.q: What does the Catholic Church teach about the Big Bang?
flashcards.a: It accepts the Big Bang as a scientific theory that does not contradict belief in God as creator.

flashcards.q: What does John 1:1-3 add to Christian beliefs about creation?
flashcards.a: It says everything was made through the Word, who is Jesus. This links creation to Jesus and the Trinity.

flashcards.q: What is the non-religious view of the universe's origin?
flashcards.a: Atheists and humanists say science, such as the Big Bang and natural laws, explains the universe without God.

flashcards.q: What is stewardship?
flashcards.a: The duty given by God to humans to look after the world and everything in it.

flashcards.q: What is dominion?
flashcards.a: The belief that humans have been given charge of the world (Genesis 1:26-28). Most believers say this means caring rule, not exploitation.

flashcards.q: Which verse is the main source for stewardship?
flashcards.a: Genesis 2:15: God put Adam in the garden 'to work it and take care of it'.

flashcards.q: What does Psalm 24:1 say and why is it important?
flashcards.a: 'The earth is the Lord's, and everything in it.' It shows the world belongs to God, so humans are caretakers, not owners.

flashcards.q: What is awe and wonder?
flashcards.a: A feeling of amazement at nature, which many believers see as showing God's greatness (Psalm 19:1).

flashcards.q: What is Tikkun Olam?
flashcards.a: The Jewish duty to repair or heal the world, which includes caring for the environment.

flashcards.q: What is bal tashchit?
flashcards.a: The Jewish rule against wasting or destroying things, based on Deuteronomy 20:19-20.

flashcards.q: Give one way a religious person could carry out the duty of stewardship.
flashcards.a: Recycle, cut energy use, plant trees, join Eco Church or support charities such as CAFOD or Christian Aid.

flashcards.q: What are natural resources?
flashcards.a: Materials found in nature that people use, such as oil, coal, gas, water and trees.

flashcards.q: What does sustainable development mean?
flashcards.a: Meeting today's needs without damaging the ability of future generations to meet theirs.

flashcards.q: Why do Christians say abusing the environment is wrong?
flashcards.a: The world belongs to God (Psalm 24:1) and humans are stewards who will answer to him, so wasting it fails in that duty.

flashcards.q: What is Laudato Si'?
flashcards.a: A 2015 letter by Pope Francis on caring for 'our common home'. It calls for less waste and pollution and care for the poor.

flashcards.q: How does the Parable of the Talents link to the environment?
flashcards.a: God entrusts humans with the world and expects them to use it wisely. Careless use fails the master.

flashcards.q: Name two pressures on the environment.
flashcards.a: Population growth and deforestation. Others: fossil fuel use, climate change, waste.

flashcards.q: What is the Jewish festival of Tu BiShvat?
flashcards.a: The New Year of the Trees, when Jews plant trees and celebrate the natural world.

flashcards.q: Which Christian groups work on environmental issues?
flashcards.a: Eco Church (A Rocha UK), CAFOD and Christian Aid.

flashcards.q: What is pollution?
flashcards.a: Contamination of the environment with harmful substances.

flashcards.q: Name three types of pollution and a cause of each.
flashcards.a: Air (vehicle and factory fumes), water (oil spills, chemicals, waste), land (rubbish and chemicals).

flashcards.q: Why do Christians say pollution is wrong?
flashcards.a: It abuses God's creation (stewardship) and harms neighbours, especially the poor, which goes against 'love your neighbour'.

flashcards.q: What effect does air pollution have on health?
flashcards.a: It can cause asthma, lung disease and other illness, and it contributes to climate change.

flashcards.q: What did the Deepwater Horizon spill (2010) show?
flashcards.a: It showed how oil pollution can kill huge numbers of sea creatures and damage ecosystems.

flashcards.q: What does Pope Francis say about pollution in Laudato Si'?
flashcards.a: That waste and pollution are damaging 'our common home' and that people must reduce waste and care for the poor.

flashcards.q: How might a Jewish person reduce pollution?
flashcards.a: By following bal tashchit (avoiding waste) and Tikkun Olam (repairing the world), for example recycling and saving energy.

flashcards.q: What is renewable energy?
flashcards.a: Energy from sources that do not run out, such as wind and solar. It reduces pollution compared to fossil fuels.

flashcards.q: What is animal experimentation?
flashcards.a: Using animals for medical research or to test products.

flashcards.q: Give a Christian argument in favour of animal experimentation.
flashcards.a: Humans are more valuable than animals (made in God's image), so research that saves lives is acceptable if suffering is minimised.

flashcards.q: Give a religious argument against animal experimentation.
flashcards.a: Animals are God's creatures and valuable to him (Genesis 1:25, Proverbs 12:10), so causing suffering is cruel and wrong.

flashcards.q: What are the 3Rs in UK animal testing?
flashcards.a: Replace animals where possible, reduce the number used, and refine methods to cut suffering.

flashcards.q: What does Genesis 9:3 say about eating animals?
flashcards.a: After the flood God said 'Everything that lives and moves about will be food for you', so Christians and Jews may eat meat.

flashcards.q: What is shechita?
flashcards.a: The Jewish method of killing animals for kosher meat, designed to be quick and humane.

flashcards.q: What is tza'ar ba'alei chayim?
flashcards.a: The Jewish teaching that humans must not cause unnecessary pain to animals.

flashcards.q: Why are some Christians vegetarian?
flashcards.a: They believe animals are God's creatures, they want to avoid cruelty, and some point to Eden (Genesis 1:29) where only plants were eaten.

flashcards.q: What does Genesis 1:27 say about human life?
flashcards.a: God created mankind in his own image. This gives humans special value and responsibility.

flashcards.q: What does Genesis 2:7 teach?
flashcards.a: God formed Adam from dust and breathed life into him. Life comes from God.

flashcards.q: What is evolution?
flashcards.a: The scientific theory that living things developed over millions of years through natural selection.

flashcards.q: Who wrote On the Origin of Species and when?
flashcards.a: Charles Darwin, in 1859.

flashcards.q: What is natural selection?
flashcards.a: Creatures best suited to their environment survive and pass on their genes, so species change over time.

flashcards.q: What is intelligent design?
flashcards.a: The belief that living things are too complex to have happened by chance, so they must have been designed by God.

flashcards.q: How can a Christian accept evolution?
flashcards.a: By saying Genesis is symbolic, that God used evolution to create life, and that Genesis explains why while science explains how.

flashcards.q: Why might a creationist reject evolution?
flashcards.a: They take Genesis literally as God's word, so God made humans directly rather than through evolution.

flashcards.q: What is the sanctity of life?
flashcards.a: The belief that life is sacred and holy because it is created by God.

flashcards.q: What is quality of life?
flashcards.a: The standard of health, comfort and happiness a person experiences.

flashcards.q: What is pikuach nefesh?
flashcards.a: The Jewish principle that saving a life overrides almost all other laws, including the Sabbath.

flashcards.q: Which commandment supports the sanctity of life?
flashcards.a: 'You shall not murder' (Exodus 20:13).

flashcards.q: Why do Christians say the body belongs to God?
flashcards.a: 1 Corinthians 6:19: 'Your bodies are temples of the Holy Spirit', so life is not ours to take.

flashcards.q: How can quality of life conflict with sanctity of life?
flashcards.a: Quality of life may suggest ending a life of suffering is kind, but sanctity of life says life is sacred whatever its condition.

flashcards.q: Give a non-religious view of the value of life.
flashcards.a: Humanists value life as the only one we have, but also stress quality of life and personal choice.

flashcards.q: What is the legal time limit for abortion in Britain?
flashcards.a: 24 weeks, under the Abortion Act 1967 as amended. After that it is only allowed in serious cases, such as risk to the mother's life or severe foetal abnormality.

flashcards.q: What does the Catholic Church teach about abortion?
flashcards.a: Life begins at conception and abortion is always wrong because it ends an innocent human life.

flashcards.q: What does the Church of England teach about abortion?
flashcards.a: Abortion takes a life and is serious, but may be the lesser of two evils in limited cases, such as a risk to the mother's life.

flashcards.q: What is the Jewish view of abortion?
flashcards.a: Life is valuable and the foetus is protected, but it is not a full person until most of it is born, so abortion is allowed to save the mother.

flashcards.q: What does pro-life mean?
flashcards.a: The belief that the unborn child has a right to life, so abortion is wrong.

flashcards.q: What does pro-choice mean?
flashcards.a: The belief that a woman has the right to choose whether to have an abortion.

flashcards.q: Which Bible verse shows God knows people before birth?
flashcards.a: Jeremiah 1:5: 'Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, before you were born I set you apart.'

flashcards.q: Give an argument for abortion that a Christian might use.
flashcards.a: Compassion: it may be the lesser of two evils where the mother's life is at risk or after rape. Jesus taught mercy.

flashcards.q: What is euthanasia?
flashcards.a: Painlessly ending someone's life to relieve suffering from an incurable or painful illness.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between voluntary and non-voluntary euthanasia?
flashcards.a: Voluntary is at the patient's request. Non-voluntary is when the patient cannot ask, for example if unconscious.

flashcards.q: What is the UK law on euthanasia?
flashcards.a: Euthanasia and assisted suicide are illegal throughout the UK (as of November 2026). The Suicide Act 1961 made suicide itself legal, but helping someone to die can bring up to 14 years in prison. The assisted dying bill fell in 2026.

flashcards.q: Why do many Christians oppose euthanasia?
flashcards.a: Life is a gift from God and only God should end it. 'You shall not murder' and the sanctity of life.

flashcards.q: What is a hospice?
flashcards.a: A place that cares for the dying, easing pain and offering support, which Christians often see as an alternative to euthanasia.

flashcards.q: Why might some Christians support euthanasia?
flashcards.a: Compassion and mercy ('Blessed are the merciful'): ending unbearable suffering may be the most loving thing.

flashcards.q: What is the Orthodox Jewish view of euthanasia?
flashcards.a: Active euthanasia is forbidden and counts as murder, but treatment that only prolongs dying may be withheld.

flashcards.q: What is a non-religious argument for euthanasia?
flashcards.a: People should have the right to choose a dignified death and avoid pointless suffering.

flashcards.q: Why do Christians believe in life after death?
flashcards.a: Jesus rose from the dead and promised eternal life (John 11:25-26), and the Bible teaches judgement, heaven and hell.

flashcards.q: What is purgatory?
flashcards.a: In Catholic belief, a place where souls are cleansed after death before they enter heaven.

flashcards.q: What is Olam Ha-Ba?
flashcards.a: The Jewish belief in a world to come after death.

flashcards.q: Why do Orthodox Jews avoid cremation?
flashcards.a: They believe God will resurrect the body, so it must be buried.

flashcards.q: How does belief in judgement affect a Christian's life?
flashcards.a: It encourages them to live morally and help others (Matthew 25:31-46), knowing God will judge them.

flashcards.q: What do atheists and humanists believe about death?
flashcards.a: That death is the end of consciousness, so this life is precious and should be lived fully.

flashcards.q: Give one argument for life after death.
flashcards.a: The resurrection of Jesus, religious experiences, near-death experiences, or the idea that the soul is separate from the body.

flashcards.q: Give one argument against life after death.
flashcards.a: There is no scientific evidence, the mind depends on the brain, and belief may be wishful thinking.

flashcards.q: Who first proposed the Big Bang theory, and why is this interesting for RE?
flashcards.a: Georges Lemaitre, a Belgian Catholic priest and physicist, in 1927. It shows a believer could see science and faith as compatible.

flashcards.q: Give two pieces of evidence for the Big Bang.
flashcards.a: Red shift (galaxies moving apart, shown by Hubble in 1929) and cosmic microwave background radiation (discovered 1964 to 1965).

flashcards.q: What did Pope Francis say about the Big Bang in 2014?
flashcards.a: That God is 'not a magician', and that the Big Bang does not contradict a divine creator but needs one.

flashcards.q: How did Rabbi Jonathan Sacks describe the relationship between science and religion?
flashcards.a: Science takes things apart to see how they work; religion puts things together to see what they mean.

flashcards.q: What is a 'Young Earth' creationist?
flashcards.a: A person who reads Genesis literally and believes the earth is only thousands of years old, made in six 24-hour days.

flashcards.q: What does 'dominion' mean?
flashcards.a: Dominance, power or control. In Genesis 1:26-28 God gives humans power over creation; most believers say it must be used responsibly.

flashcards.q: What is the Shmita year?
flashcards.a: Every seventh year, when the Torah says the land should rest and not be farmed (Leviticus 25:4).

flashcards.q: What does Midrash Kohelet Rabbah 7:13 teach?
flashcards.a: God shows Adam the world and says: do not ruin and destroy my world, for if you do there is no one to repair it after you.

flashcards.q: What did the Church of England decide in 2020 about carbon emissions?
flashcards.a: General Synod set a target of net zero carbon by 2030.

flashcards.q: How might a humanist explain the duty to protect the world?
flashcards.a: It is the only home humans and other life have, and future generations deserve a healthy planet. The duty comes from reason and compassion, not God.

flashcards.q: What is the difference between renewable and non-renewable resources?
flashcards.a: Renewable resources do not run out (wind, solar, wave); non-renewable ones will run out (coal, oil, gas).

flashcards.q: What does Leviticus 25:23 teach about the land?
flashcards.a: 'The land is mine and you reside in my land as foreigners and strangers': God owns the land, humans are tenants.

flashcards.q: What is the Paris Agreement (2015)?
flashcards.a: An international treaty to limit global warming to well below 2 degrees Celsius by cutting greenhouse gas emissions.

flashcards.q: What did Pope Francis call for in Laudato Si'?
flashcards.a: 'Ecological conversion': a change of heart and lifestyle to care for 'our common home', especially for the sake of the poor.

flashcards.q: Give one way religious believers can help to reduce pollution.
flashcards.a: Use public transport, walk or cycle (accept: recycle, cut single-use plastic, save energy, join a litter pick, install solar panels).

flashcards.q: What did Laudato Si' say the earth was beginning to look like?
flashcards.a: 'An immense pile of filth' (paragraph 21), because of waste and a throwaway culture.

flashcards.q: What are microplastics?
flashcards.a: Tiny pieces of plastic from broken-down waste that enter seas, soil and food chains.

flashcards.q: Name a UK law or policy to reduce pollution.
flashcards.a: The Climate Change Act 2008 (net zero by 2050) or the plastic bag charge (5p in 2015, now 10p).

flashcards.q: What are the 3Rs in UK animal research?
flashcards.a: Replace animals where possible, reduce the number used, and refine methods to reduce suffering.

flashcards.q: What does the Catechism (CCC 2417) say about animal experiments?
flashcards.a: They are morally acceptable within reasonable limits if they help to care for or save human lives.

flashcards.q: How many scientific procedures on animals were carried out in Great Britain in 2025?
flashcards.a: About 2.54 million, the lowest since the 1986 Act; most used mice (Home Office).

flashcards.q: Since when has testing cosmetics on animals been banned in the UK?
What is 'speciesism'?
flashcards.a: Peter Singer's term for treating one species as more important just because of its species, for example ignoring animal suffering to benefit humans.

flashcards.q: Who helped found the RSPCA in 1824?
flashcards.a: A group including the Anglican priest Arthur Broome.

flashcards.q: What did Pope John Paul II say about evolution in 1996?
flashcards.a: That evolution is 'more than a hypothesis', while the soul is created directly by God.

flashcards.q: What is theistic evolution?
flashcards.a: The belief that God created life through the process of evolution.

flashcards.q: What does the 'breath of life' in Genesis 2:7 suggest?
flashcards.a: Human life comes directly from God, who gives each person a soul.

flashcards.q: Give two pieces of evidence for evolution.
flashcards.a: Fossils and DNA (accept: similar body structures in different species; observed natural selection).

flashcards.q: What is situation ethics?
flashcards.a: Joseph Fletcher's idea (1966) that Christians should do the most loving thing (agape) in each situation rather than follow fixed rules.

flashcards.q: What is the principle of utility?
flashcards.a: The right action is the one that brings the greatest good (happiness) for the greatest number.

flashcards.q: What does Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5 teach?
flashcards.a: Whoever saves a single life is as if they saved an entire world: every life has infinite value.

flashcards.q: What does Job 1:21 say and how is it used?
flashcards.a: 'The Lord gave and the Lord has taken away': only God should decide when life begins and ends.

flashcards.q: Give one criticism of the quality of life argument.
flashcards.a: It could suggest some lives, such as those of disabled people, are worth less than others.

flashcards.q: What changed in April 2026 in abortion law in England and Wales?
flashcards.a: The Crime and Policing Act 2026 means a woman can no longer be prosecuted for ending her own pregnancy, and past convictions are pardoned. The Abortion Act 1967 rules for doctors remain.

flashcards.q: Under the Abortion Act, when can abortion happen after 24 weeks?
flashcards.a: If the woman's life is at risk, there is a risk of grave permanent injury to her, or a substantial risk of serious disability in the baby.

flashcards.q: What is the principle of double effect?
flashcards.a: The Catholic idea that an action with a good aim, such as saving the mother's life, may be allowed even if a bad result (the foetus dying) is foreseen but not intended.

flashcards.q: What does Mishnah Oholot 7:6 teach about abortion?
flashcards.a: If the birth endangers the mother, her life comes before the foetus's life; but once most of the baby is born it cannot be harmed.

flashcards.q: What is viability?
flashcards.a: The point at which a foetus could survive outside the womb, around 24 weeks.

flashcards.q: How many abortions were there for residents of England and Wales in 2023?
flashcards.a: About 278,000 (DHSC); 87% were medical (pill) abortions.

flashcards.q: What happened to the assisted dying bill for England and Wales in 2026?
flashcards.a: It ran out of time in the House of Lords in April 2026; a new version was defeated in the Commons on 11 September 2026 (286 to 270). Assisted dying remains illegal (as of November 2026).

flashcards.q: What is the difference between active and passive euthanasia?
flashcards.a: Active: deliberately doing something to end life (a lethal injection). Passive: withdrawing or withholding treatment so the person dies of their illness.

flashcards.q: Who started the modern hospice movement?
flashcards.a: Dame Cicely Saunders, a Christian, who opened St Christopher's Hospice in London in 1967.

flashcards.q: What does the Catechism allow at the end of life?
flashcards.a: Stopping 'burdensome, dangerous, extraordinary' treatment and giving pain relief, though deliberately ending life is wrong (CCC 2277 to 2278).

flashcards.q: Name two Christian leaders who have supported assisted dying.
flashcards.a: Former Archbishop of Canterbury Lord Carey and Archbishop Desmond Tutu.

flashcards.q: Give a non-religious argument against euthanasia.
flashcards.a: Vulnerable people might feel pressured, diagnoses can be wrong, and it could lead to a 'slippery slope' towards non-voluntary euthanasia.

flashcards.q: Why do Jewish mourners say Kaddish for eleven months?
flashcards.a: Tradition says a soul may be purified in Gehinnom for up to twelve months; saying it for eleven shows confidence the person was not wicked.

flashcards.q: How does belief in an afterlife affect beliefs about the value of human life?
flashcards.a: Life is a gift leading to eternity and judgement, so it is precious, must be used well and should not be ended early.

flashcards.q: How do humanists say people live on after death?
flashcards.a: Through their children, achievements and the memories of others; humanist funerals celebrate the life lived.

flashcards.q: What do Protestants mainly believe about salvation?
flashcards.a: It comes through faith in Jesus and God's grace, not by earning it; most reject purgatory.

quiz.why: Creation by God is the religious explanation. Red shift and background radiation are evidence for the Big Bang; natural selection is about evolution.

quiz.why: The Big Bang theory describes the expansion of the universe from a hot, dense point.

quiz.q: Which Jewish idea means 'repairing the world'?

options: Meet today's needs without harming future generations

quiz.q: Which parable is used to teach that humans should use God's gifts wisely?

quiz.q: Pope Francis's 2015 letter about caring for the environment is called:

quiz.q: Which is an example of water pollution?

quiz.q: What does 'kosher' mean?

quiz.q: Which statement is a religious argument against animal experimentation?
options: Animals are God's creatures and should not suffer
It is legal in the UK

quiz.q: Which Bible verse shows God knew people before they were born?
quiz.why: Jeremiah 1:5 is widely used in the abortion debate.

A patient asks a doctor to end their life

quiz.q: What is a hospice?
options: A place that cares for the dying

quiz.q: Which commandment is used to argue euthanasia is wrong?

quiz.q: Which Christian belief is a place where souls are cleansed before heaven?

quiz.q: Which verse describes Jesus saying 'I am the resurrection and the life'?

quiz.why: Fossil fuels such as coal will run out.

quiz.q: 'The land is mine and you reside in my land as foreigners and strangers.' Which teaching does this support?

quiz.q: What does the Paris Agreement (2015) aim to do?

quiz.q: Which is a way to reduce pollution rather than a teaching about it?

quiz.why: Sewage contaminates water.

The commandment is about human life

quiz.why: Theistic evolution accepts both God and evolution.

quiz.q: Which Bible verse says God 'breathed into his nostrils the breath of life'?

options: The mind depends on the brain

options: Life is more precious because it is the only one
