exam.q: 'Abortion is always wrong.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you: should give reasoned arguments in support of this statement; should give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; should refer to religious arguments; may refer to non-religious arguments; should reach a justified conclusion.
exam.model:
Many religious people agree with this statement. The Roman Catholic Church teaches that life begins at conception and is sacred because humans are made in God's image (Genesis 1:27). Jeremiah 1:5 says 'Before I formed you in the womb I knew you', which suggests God has a plan for every unborn child, and the commandment 'You shall not murder' (Exodus 20:13) is used to say abortion is killing. Pro-life supporters add that unwanted children can be adopted. This is a strong argument for believers who see life as a gift from God, because it treats the unborn as having full value from the start.

However, many people disagree. The Church of England teaches that abortion is serious, but may be the lesser of two evils where the mother's life is at risk, or after rape. Jesus taught compassion ('Blessed are the merciful', Matthew 5:7), so some Christians say the suffering of the woman matters too. Judaism teaches that the mother's life comes first and that the foetus is not a full person until it is mostly born. Pro-choice supporters argue that a woman has the right to decide what happens to her own body and that quality of life matters, for example if a baby would be born with a severe condition. This argument is strong in extreme cases such as danger to life, but it is less convincing if the reason is only convenience, as it does not explain the rights of the unborn child.

In conclusion, I think the word 'always' makes the statement too strong. Even religious teaching recognises exceptions, such as saving the mother's life, and a loving God would not want a woman to die. However, I think the sanctity of life means abortion should never be taken lightly, and Christians would say it should be a last resort with support and alternatives offered. Therefore abortion is a serious moral wrong in most cases, but not in every case.
for: Catholic teaching: life begins at conception and is sacred (Genesis 1:27, Catechism).
Jeremiah 1:5 and Psalm 139:13: God knows and plans each person before birth.
'You shall not murder' (Exodus 20:13): abortion is killing an innocent life.
Alternatives such as adoption exist.
Evaluation: strong for those who accept sanctity of life, since the unborn child has full value.
against: Church of England: lesser of two evils, for example if the mother's life is at risk.
Compassion: Matthew 5:7, and Jewish teaching that the mother's life comes first.
Pro-choice: the woman's right to choose, and quality of life.
Evaluation: strong in extreme cases, weaker if the reason is convenience.
exam.conclusion: Abortion is a serious wrong in most views, but 'always' is too strong as even religious teachings allow exceptions such as saving the mother's life.

exam.q: 'Euthanasia should be legal.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you: should give reasoned arguments in support of this statement; should give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; should refer to religious arguments; may refer to non-religious arguments; should reach a justified conclusion.
exam.model:
Some people believe euthanasia should be legal. Non-religious people, such as humanists, argue that people should be able to choose a dignified death and avoid pointless suffering, as they have a right to decide about their own lives. Some Christians agree, quoting 'Blessed are the merciful' (Matthew 5:7): if a person is in unbearable pain and clearly asks to die, helping them could be the most loving act. God gave humans free will, so they should be able to decide how they die. This argument is strong because it is based on compassion and autonomy, but it relies on there being safeguards so the choice is truly free.

However, many people think euthanasia should remain illegal. The Catholic Church and Church of England teach that life is a gift from God and only God should end it. Exodus 20:13 says 'You shall not murder', and 1 Corinthians 6:19 says our bodies are 'temples of the Holy Spirit'. Orthodox Jews also see euthanasia as murder. They argue that hospices and palliative care can control pain without ending life. Many people also worry that if euthanasia were legal, the elderly, disabled or poor might feel pressured to choose it, or that mistakes might be made. This argument is strong because the risk of pressure on vulnerable people is real, and it is hard to reverse the choice once made.

In conclusion, I think the arguments against are slightly stronger. Compassion is important, but the sanctity of life and the risk of harm to vulnerable people mean that changing the law is dangerous. Better palliative care is a safer way to reduce suffering. However, I accept that people who are dying and in great pain can have a powerful case, so the law needs to be debated carefully, and religious and non-religious people can reasonably disagree.
for: Compassion and mercy (Matthew 5:7): ending unbearable suffering can be loving.
Free will and autonomy: people should choose how they die.
Humanists: a right to a dignified death.
Evaluation: strong, but needs safeguards to make sure the choice is free.
against: Sanctity of life: only God should end life (Exodus 20:13, 1 Corinthians 6:19).
Orthodox Jews: active euthanasia is murder.
Hospices and palliative care are alternatives.
Risk of pressure on vulnerable people and mistakes.
Evaluation: strong because the risks are serious and irreversible.
exam.conclusion: Compassion gives a powerful case, but the sanctity of life and the risk to vulnerable people make the arguments against slightly stronger.

exam.q: 'There is no good evidence for life after death.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you: should give reasoned arguments in support of this statement; should give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; should refer to religious arguments; may refer to non-religious arguments; should reach a justified conclusion.
exam.model:
Many non-religious people agree with this statement. Atheists and humanists say there is no scientific proof that anything happens after death, because nobody has been able to test it. They also point out that the mind depends on the brain, so when the brain stops, consciousness ends. Some say belief in heaven is just wishful thinking, because people find it hard to accept death. This argument is strong because science relies on evidence that can be tested, but it does not prove that there is no afterlife, only that science cannot measure it.

However, religious people argue that there is good evidence. Christians point to the resurrection of Jesus, who rose from the dead and promised 'I am the resurrection and the life' (John 11:25). If Jesus rose, death is not the end. Many believers also cite religious experiences, and some people report near-death experiences. Christians and Jews also say that conscience and the sense that justice must be done suggest God will judge people after death (Matthew 25:31-46). Orthodox Jews believe God will raise the dead. This argument is strong for believers who accept the Bible as God's word, but is weaker for sceptics, as the resurrection depends on faith in the Gospels and near-death experiences could be caused by the brain.

In conclusion, I think the statement depends on what counts as 'good evidence'. If it means scientific proof, the statement is true, as there is none. But religious believers use a different kind of evidence, such as scripture and experience, which they find convincing. I think belief in life after death is reasonable, but it cannot be proved, so it ultimately requires faith. For someone who already believes in God, the resurrection is strong evidence. For someone who does not, it is not.
for: No scientific proof of an afterlife.
The mind depends on the brain, so consciousness ends at death.
Heaven may be wishful thinking.
Evaluation: strong because science needs testable evidence, but it does not prove there is no afterlife.
against: Resurrection of Jesus and his promise (John 11:25).
Religious experiences and near-death experiences.
Conscience and justice suggest judgement (Matthew 25:31-46); Orthodox Jewish belief in resurrection.
Evaluation: strong for believers, weaker for sceptics who point to the brain.
exam.conclusion: There is no scientific proof, but believers use scripture and experience as evidence, so belief is reasonable but requires faith.

exam.q: 'Looking after the environment is the most important duty for religious believers.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you: should give reasoned arguments in support of this statement; should give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; should refer to religious arguments; may refer to non-religious arguments; should reach a justified conclusion.
exam.model:
Some religious people would agree with this statement. Christians and Jews believe God created the world and it belongs to him ('The earth is the Lord's', Psalm 24:1), so humans are stewards who must look after it. In Genesis 2:15 God told Adam to 'take care of' the garden. Jews also follow Tikkun Olam, repairing the world. If the environment is destroyed, there will be no future for humans or other creatures, so protecting it comes before everything else. This is a strong argument because environmental damage such as climate change affects everyone, especially the poor, and cannot easily be reversed.

However, other believers say it is not the most important duty. Jesus said the greatest commandments are to love God and love your neighbour (Matthew 22:37-39), so worshipping God and caring for people come first. Christians may argue that helping the poor, the sick and the homeless is more urgent than protecting nature, and that humans are more valuable than the rest of creation because they are made in God's image. Some believers also think that since God is in control, humans cannot be the only ones responsible. This argument is strong because Jesus put people first, but it is weaker when we remember that harming the environment also harms people, so the two duties are linked.

In conclusion, I think looking after the environment is a very important duty but not necessarily the most important one. Religious teaching puts loving God and loving others first, but caring for the environment is a way of doing both, because it respects God's creation and protects human life. For this reason I believe the duties support each other, and a believer who ignores the environment is failing in other duties as well.
for: The world is God's (Psalm 24:1) and humans are stewards (Genesis 2:15).
Tikkun Olam: Jews must repair the world.
Without a healthy planet, there is no future for humans.
Evaluation: strong because environmental damage affects everyone and is hard to reverse.
against: Greatest commandments: love God and love neighbour (Matthew 22:37-39).
Helping people may be more urgent than protecting nature; humans are made in God's image.
Evaluation: strong because Jesus put people first, but environmental harm also harms people.
exam.conclusion: Looking after the environment is very important, but it is part of loving God and neighbour, so the duties go together rather than competing.

exam.q: 'Science has disproved what religion teaches about the origins of the universe.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you: should give reasoned arguments in support of this statement; should give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; should refer to religious arguments; may refer to non-religious arguments; should reach a justified conclusion.
exam.model:
Some people agree with this statement. Genesis 1 teaches that God created the world in six days, but the Big Bang theory says the universe began almost 14 billion years ago and developed through natural processes. Scientists can support the Big Bang with evidence, such as the expansion of the universe, while there is no scientific evidence for the six days. Non-religious people, such as atheists, say that science explains the universe without needing God. This argument is strong for those who only trust evidence, because the Big Bang is supported by testable observations.

However, many religious people disagree. Creationist Christians and some Orthodox Jews say Genesis is the word of God, so it is true and science is mistaken. Others say there is no conflict at all. Catholics and liberal Christians accept the Big Bang and say Genesis is a symbolic story. They believe that God caused the Big Bang, so science explains how the universe began and religion explains why. The Big Bang theory was even first proposed by a Catholic priest, Georges Lemaitre. Science also cannot explain what caused the Big Bang or why anything exists at all. This argument is strong because it respects both sides, but it does not satisfy creationists who think the Bible should be taken literally.

In conclusion, I do not think science has disproved religion. Science may have disproved a literal reading of Genesis for some believers, but religion is not mainly about how the universe began. It is about why it exists and what it means. Since science cannot answer questions of purpose or what came before the Big Bang, belief in a creator God remains possible. Therefore the statement is too strong, although it does challenge those who read Genesis literally.
for: Genesis says six days; science says almost 14 billion years.
The Big Bang is supported by evidence; Genesis is not scientific evidence.
Non-religious: the universe can be explained naturally without God.
Evaluation: strong for those who trust only evidence.
against: Many Christians and Jews read Genesis as symbolic and accept the Big Bang.
Science explains how, religion explains why; Georges Lemaitre, a priest, proposed the Big Bang.
Science cannot explain what caused the Big Bang or why anything exists.
Creationists say Genesis is God's word.
Evaluation: strong because it respects both, though it does not satisfy literal believers.
exam.conclusion: Science challenges a literal reading of Genesis but has not disproved belief in a creator, so the statement is too strong.

exam.q: Explain two different religious beliefs about euthanasia. In your answer you must refer to one or more religious traditions.

Abuse is wrong because the earth is God's (1), development (1), Leviticus 25:23 or Psalm 24:1 (1), application (1).

Judgement (1), development (1), Matthew 25:31-46 (1), application (1).

Liberal Christian or Reform Jewish: may be acceptable (1), compassion / Matthew 5:7 / autonomy with safeguards (1).

points: Christian: the world belongs to God / humans are caretakers (1), Psalm 24:1 / Genesis 2:15 / accountable to God (1).
Jewish: duty to care for and repair the world (1), Tikkun Olam / bal tashchit / Midrash Kohelet Rabbah 7:13 (1).
Other creditable: future generations; the poor suffer most from damage.

points: Christian: use resources carefully as stewards (1), Psalm 24:1 / Parable of the Talents / Laudato Si' (1).
Jewish: do not waste (1), bal tashchit / Deuteronomy 20:19 / Leviticus 25:23 land belongs to God (1).

Liberal Christian or Reform Jewish: quality of life matters (1), compassion / situation ethics / avoiding suffering (1).

This is because Reform Judaism focuses on living a good life now by following the mitzvot, and many Reform Jews accept cremation.

Protestant: salvation through faith, no purgatory (1); Orthodox Jewish: resurrection in the Messianic age, burial (1); Reform Jewish: the soul lives on, focus on this life (1).
Two different beliefs, each developed, for 4 marks.

exam.q: Explain two religious beliefs about the origins of the universe. Refer to sacred writings or another source of religious belief and teaching in your answer.
exam.model: One belief is that God created the universe out of nothing, simply by speaking. Genesis 1:3 says 'And God said, Let there be light, and there was light.' This means Christians and Jews believe God is all-powerful and the universe depends on him, so many praise God as creator in worship. Another belief is that the Big Bang can be the way God created the universe. Many Christians read Genesis as a symbolic story rather than a scientific account. Pope Francis said in 2014 that the Big Bang does not contradict a divine creator but needs one. This means Catholics can accept science while believing God started the universe for a purpose.
points: God created ex nihilo / by his word (1), developed: omnipotence, the universe depends on God (1).
Source: Genesis 1:1, Genesis 1:3 or Hebrews 11:3 (1), applied (1).
Big Bang as God's method / Genesis symbolic (1), developed: science explains how, religion why (1).
Source: Pope Francis 2014, John 1:3, or Lemaitre as a Catholic priest (1), applied (1).

exam.q: Explain two religious beliefs about why believers should help to reduce pollution. Refer to sacred writings or another source of religious belief and teaching in your answer.
exam.model: One belief is that the world belongs to God, so polluting it abuses something he has entrusted to us. Psalm 24:1 says 'The earth is the Lord's, and everything in it.' This means Christians and Jews are stewards who must keep the world clean, so they might recycle, cut plastic use and join schemes such as Eco Church. Another belief is that pollution harms other people, especially the poor and future generations. Jesus taught 'Love your neighbour as yourself' (Matthew 22:39). This means Christians should reduce air and water pollution that damages people's health, for example by walking or cycling instead of driving and campaigning for cleaner rivers.
points: Stewardship / God owns the world (1), developed: polluting abuses God's gift (1).
Source: Psalm 24:1, Genesis 2:15 or Laudato Si' (1), applied to pollution (1).
Pollution harms neighbours, the poor and future generations (1), developed with an example (1).
Source: Matthew 22:39 or bal tashchit (Deuteronomy 20:19) (1), applied (1).

exam.q: Explain two religious beliefs about the origins of human life. Refer to sacred writings or another source of religious belief and teaching in your answer.
exam.model: One belief is that God created humans directly and specially. Genesis 2:7 says God 'formed a man from the dust of the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life'. This means creationist Christians believe Adam and Eve were real people made by God, and that each human has a soul given by God. Another belief is that God created humans through evolution. Catholics accept that the human body may have evolved, but teach that each soul is created directly by God, and Genesis 1:27 says humans are made 'in his own image'. This means Catholics can accept Darwin's science while still believing human life is sacred and has a purpose.
points: God created humans directly (1), developed: creationism / Adam and Eve literal (1).
Source: Genesis 2:7 (1), applied: humans have a God-given soul (1).
God used evolution (1), developed: Genesis symbolic, Catholic view on the soul (1).
Source: Genesis 1:27, Pope John Paul II 1996 or Psalm 139:13 (1), applied (1).

exam.q: Explain two religious beliefs about abortion when the mother's life is at risk. Refer to sacred writings or another source of religious belief and teaching in your answer.
exam.model: One belief, held by Jews, is that the mother's life must come first. The Mishnah teaches that if a woman is having difficulty giving birth, her life comes before the life of the foetus (Mishnah Oholot 7:6). This means that in Judaism abortion is not just allowed but required when the mother would otherwise die, because the foetus is not yet a full person. Another belief, held by Catholics, is that a doctor may treat the mother even if the baby dies as a result, but must not directly intend to kill the baby. This is the principle of double effect. The Catechism teaches that life must be protected from conception (CCC 2270), so a Catholic doctor may remove a cancerous womb to save the mother, accepting but not aiming at the death of the foetus.
points: Jewish: mother's life comes first (1), developed: foetus not a full person until birth (1).
Source: Mishnah Oholot 7:6 or Exodus 21:22 (1), applied: abortion is required (1).
Catholic: double effect, treatment allowed but not direct abortion (1), developed with an example such as an ectopic pregnancy or cancerous womb (1).
Source: CCC 2270 or Exodus 20:13 (1), applied (1). Church of England 'lesser of two evils' also creditable.

exam.q: 'Humans have the right to use the world however they want.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you: should give reasoned arguments in support of this statement; should give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; should refer to religious arguments; may refer to non-religious arguments; should reach a justified conclusion.
exam.model:
Some people might agree with this statement. In Genesis 1:28 God tells humans to 'rule over' the fish, birds and every living creature, which is called dominion. A minority of Christians have read this as meaning the world was made for human use, so humans may use its resources as they need. Some non-religious people also argue that humans are the most intelligent species and that economic growth, which uses natural resources, lifts people out of poverty. This argument has some strength because humans do need to use the world to survive, for food, energy and shelter. However, it is weak if it means 'however they want', because uncontrolled use has led to climate change and pollution that harm humans themselves.

Most religious believers strongly disagree. Psalm 24:1 says 'The earth is the Lord's, and everything in it', so humans do not own the world; they are stewards who look after it for God. Genesis 2:15 says God put Adam in the garden 'to work it and take care of it'. Jews follow bal tashchit, which forbids needless destruction, and Tikkun Olam, the duty to repair the world. Pope Francis in Laudato Si' called the earth 'our common home' and said its abuse hurts the poor most. Humanists also disagree: although they do not believe in God, they argue we have a responsibility to other species and to future generations who will inherit the planet. This argument is very strong because it is shared by religious and non-religious people and is supported by scientific evidence about environmental damage.

In conclusion, I disagree with the statement. Humans clearly have a right to use the world to meet their needs, but not to use it 'however they want'. Even dominion is best understood as responsible rule, like a good king caring for his people. Because the world belongs to God for believers, and to future generations for humanists, its use must be careful and sustainable.
for: Dominion: Genesis 1:28 gives humans power over creation.
Humans need natural resources for food, energy and development.
Some argue human needs and economic growth come first.
Evaluation: true that humans may use the world, but 'however they want' ignores harm.
against: Stewardship: Psalm 24:1 and Genesis 2:15; humans are caretakers, not owners.
Jewish bal tashchit and Tikkun Olam forbid waste and call for repair.
Laudato Si': abuse of 'our common home' harms the poor.
Humanists: duty to future generations and other species.
Evaluation: strong because shared by religious and non-religious people and backed by science.
exam.conclusion: Humans may use the world to meet their needs, but not however they want: dominion means responsible rule, so use must be sustainable.

exam.q: 'Religious believers should do more than anyone else to stop pollution.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you: should give reasoned arguments in support of this statement; should give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; should refer to religious arguments; may refer to non-religious arguments; should reach a justified conclusion.
exam.model:
Some people agree with this statement. Christians and Jews believe the world belongs to God (Psalm 24:1), and that God gave humans the job of stewards, to 'work it and take care of it' (Genesis 2:15). If someone believes the earth is God's creation and that they will be judged on how they treated it, as in the Parable of the Talents, then they have an extra reason to care. Pope Francis's Laudato Si' says the earth is starting to look like 'an immense pile of filth' and calls believers to 'ecological conversion'. Jews also have the rule of bal tashchit against waste. This argument is strong because believers have both religious duties and practical networks, such as Eco Church, to make a difference.

On the other hand, many people would say pollution is everyone's responsibility equally. Pollution harms the health of everyone, through asthma, polluted rivers and climate change, so everyone has a reason to stop it, religious or not. Humanists argue from reason and compassion that we owe future generations a clean planet, and many environmental campaigners have no religion. Also, the biggest causes of pollution come from industry and transport, so governments and businesses, through laws such as the Climate Change Act 2008, can do far more than individual believers. Some Christians would agree, saying 'love your neighbour' means working together with everyone rather than competing. This argument is strong because it focuses on results rather than on who has the strongest motive.

In conclusion, I think religious believers do have extra reasons to stop pollution, because they see the world as God's gift and believe they are accountable to him. However, it is not fair to say they should do more than anyone else, as pollution affects everyone and needs everyone's effort, especially governments. The best view is that believers should set an example and work alongside others, rather than carry the burden alone.
for: Stewardship: Psalm 24:1, Genesis 2:15; believers are accountable to God (Parable of the Talents).
Laudato Si' calls for 'ecological conversion'.
Jewish bal tashchit and Tikkun Olam.
Believers have networks such as Eco Church, A Rocha and CAFOD.
Evaluation: strong because believers have extra motives and means.
against: Pollution harms everyone, so everyone is equally responsible.
Humanists: duty to future generations from reason and compassion.
Governments and businesses cause and can cut the most pollution (Climate Change Act 2008, Paris Agreement).
'Love your neighbour' suggests working together, not competing.
Evaluation: strong because it focuses on results.
exam.conclusion: Believers have extra reasons to act and should set an example, but pollution is everyone's responsibility, especially governments, so they should not be expected to do more than anyone else.

exam.q: 'It is wrong to use animals for medical research.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you: should give reasoned arguments in support of this statement; should give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; should refer to religious arguments; may refer to non-religious arguments; should reach a justified conclusion.
exam.model:
Some religious believers agree with this statement. They argue that animals are God's creatures, which he saw were 'good' (Genesis 1:25), and Jesus taught that not one sparrow is forgotten by God (Luke 12:6). Proverbs 12:10 says 'The righteous care for the needs of their animals.' Christians such as the theologian Andrew Linzey argue animals have God-given worth, so causing them pain for human benefit abuses dominion. Non-religious thinkers like Peter Singer say favouring humans simply because they are human is 'speciesism', and animal rights groups point out that results from animals do not always apply to humans and that alternatives, such as computer models and human cell cultures, now exist. This argument is strong because animals can clearly suffer, and the UK government itself has a strategy to replace animal tests.

On the other hand, many religious believers think some animal research is justified. The Catholic Catechism (2417) says experiments on animals are morally acceptable 'within reasonable limits' if they help to care for or save human lives, because humans are made in God's image and have greater value. Orthodox Jews also allow research that is truly needed to save human life (pikuach nefesh), as long as pain is minimised (tza'ar ba'alei chayim). Many medicines and vaccines were developed with animal research, and UK law requires the 3Rs to reduce suffering. A utilitarian would say the suffering of a smaller number of animals is outweighed by the lives of millions of people saved. This is a strong argument because the benefit to human life is real and the research is closely controlled.

In conclusion, I disagree that it is always wrong. Where research is necessary to save human lives, there are no alternatives, and suffering is kept to a minimum, religious teaching on the special value of human life makes it acceptable. However, the argument against reminds us that animals matter to God, so research should be replaced wherever possible.
for: Animals are God's creatures (Genesis 1:25, Luke 12:6, Proverbs 12:10).
Andrew Linzey: animals have God-given worth; experiments abuse dominion.
Peter Singer: speciesism; animal suffering counts equally.
Alternatives exist and animal results do not always apply to humans.
Evaluation: strong because animals clearly suffer.
against: Catechism 2417: acceptable within reasonable limits to save human lives.
Humans are made in God's image and have greater value.
Orthodox Judaism: allowed for pikuach nefesh if pain is minimised.
Medicines and vaccines; strict UK law (3Rs); utilitarian benefit.
Evaluation: strong because human lives are saved under controls.
exam.conclusion: Not always wrong: necessary research with minimal suffering is acceptable, but animals matter to God so it should be replaced wherever possible.

exam.q: 'Evolution proves that God did not create human life.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you: should give reasoned arguments in support of this statement; should give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; should refer to religious arguments; may refer to non-religious arguments; should reach a justified conclusion.
exam.model:
Some people agree with this statement. Atheists such as Richard Dawkins argue that Darwin's theory of evolution by natural selection fully explains how humans developed from earlier species over millions of years, with strong evidence from fossils and DNA. If complex living things, including humans, can be explained by natural processes, there is no need for a creator. Evolution also contradicts a literal reading of Genesis, in which God made Adam from dust and Eve from his rib in a single day. This argument is strong because the scientific evidence for evolution is overwhelming and accepted by nearly all scientists.

However, many religious believers disagree. The Catholic Church accepts evolution: Pope John Paul II said in 1996 it is 'more than a hypothesis', but taught that God creates each human soul directly. Many Christians and Jews read Genesis as a symbolic story that teaches why humans exist, that they are made 'in his own image' (Genesis 1:27), not a scientific account of how. This view is called theistic evolution: God used evolution as his method. Rabbi Jonathan Sacks argued that science explains how things work, while religion explains what they mean. Even creationists who reject evolution would disagree with the statement, though for different reasons, as they believe Genesis is literally true. This argument is strong because evolution describes a process, and a process cannot by itself show whether or not there is a God behind it.

In conclusion, I disagree with the statement. Evolution is very good evidence against a literal reading of Genesis, but it does not prove that God did not create human life. Believers who see God working through evolution are not contradicting science, and the question of why there is life at all, and why humans can love and think morally, is not something evolution can answer. The word 'proves' is therefore too strong.
for: Darwin's natural selection explains human origins naturally (fossils, DNA).
Richard Dawkins: no need for a designer.
Evolution contradicts a literal reading of Genesis 2.
Evaluation: strong scientific evidence.
against: Catholic Church accepts evolution; God creates each soul (John Paul II, 1996).
Genesis is symbolic: humans in God's image (Genesis 1:27); theistic evolution.
Rabbi Sacks: science explains how, religion what it means.
Creationists reject evolution itself.
Evaluation: a process cannot prove there is no God behind it.
exam.conclusion: Evolution counts against a literal Genesis but does not prove God did not create human life, so 'proves' is too strong.

exam.q: 'The quality of a person's life is more important than the sanctity of life.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you: should give reasoned arguments in support of this statement; should give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; should refer to religious arguments; may refer to non-religious arguments; should reach a justified conclusion.
exam.model:
Some people agree with this statement. Humanists argue that life is valuable because of what a person can experience and enjoy, so if a life is full of unbearable pain with no hope of improvement, its quality matters more than an abstract idea of sacredness. Some liberal Christians use situation ethics, which says Christians should do the most loving (agape) thing in each situation; Jesus healed the sick and showed compassion ('Blessed are the merciful', Matthew 5:7). A utilitarian would also weigh the suffering of everyone affected. This argument is strong in extreme cases, such as terminal illness, where keeping someone alive may only prolong suffering.

On the other hand, many believers think the sanctity of life is more important. Christians and Jews believe all humans are made in God's image (Genesis 1:27), and that 'the Lord gave and the Lord has taken away' (Job 1:21), so only God should decide when life ends. The Catholic Church teaches that life is sacred from conception to natural death, whatever its quality. Judaism teaches that saving one life is like saving a whole world (Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5). Critics of the quality of life view, including many disability rights groups, also warn that it could suggest some lives, such as those of disabled or elderly people, are worth less, and that judgements about quality can be wrong. This argument is strong because it protects the most vulnerable people and gives every life equal value.

In conclusion, I think the sanctity of life should remain the more important principle, because it treats every person as equally valuable and protects the vulnerable. However, quality of life should not be ignored: even the Catholic Church allows strong pain relief and stopping burdensome treatment, which shows compassion for quality of life within the limits of sanctity. So both matter, but sanctity should set the boundaries.
for: Humanists: life's value lies in experience and wellbeing.
Situation ethics: do the most loving thing; Matthew 5:7.
Utilitarian weighing of suffering.
Evaluation: strong in extreme cases of suffering.
against: Genesis 1:27: all made in God's image; Job 1:21: only God ends life.
Catholic teaching: sacred from conception to natural death.
Mishnah Sanhedrin 4:5: each life is like a whole world.
Quality judgements may devalue disabled or elderly people.
Evaluation: strong because it protects the vulnerable.
exam.conclusion: Sanctity of life should set the limits because it protects every person equally, but compassion for quality of life matters within those limits.

exam.q: 'Religious believers should accept abortion if the mother's life is at risk.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you: should give reasoned arguments in support of this statement; should give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view; should refer to religious arguments; may refer to non-religious arguments; should reach a justified conclusion.
exam.model:
Many religious believers agree with this statement. Judaism teaches that if a birth endangers the mother, 'her life comes before the life of the foetus' (Mishnah Oholot 7:6), so abortion is not just allowed but required, because the foetus is not yet a full person. The Church of England teaches that abortion may be the lesser of two evils in strictly limited cases, such as a serious risk to the mother's life. Many Christians also point out that if the mother dies, the baby will often die too, so saving one life is better than losing both. Compassion ('Blessed are the merciful', Matthew 5:7) and the sanctity of the mother's life both support this. This is a strong argument because it uses the sanctity of life on both sides, not just quality of life.

On the other hand, the Catholic Church teaches that direct abortion is always wrong, because life must be protected 'absolutely from the moment of conception' (CCC 2270), and two lives are equally sacred. Some pro-life Christians argue that doctors should try to save both lives, and that deliberately ending one innocent life to save another is still killing. However, even Catholics accept the principle of double effect: treatment to save the mother, such as removing an ectopic pregnancy or a cancerous womb, is allowed if the foetus's death is foreseen but not intended. This argument is strong because it refuses to treat any life as less valuable, but in practice it reaches a similar result in the most serious cases.

In conclusion, I agree with the statement. Almost all religious traditions, including Judaism, the Church of England and even Catholicism through double effect, accept that the mother's life can be saved even if the foetus dies. The disagreement is mainly about whether the death can be directly intended, not about whether the mother should be allowed to die. Therefore religious believers can and should accept life-saving treatment in this situation.
for: Judaism: the mother's life comes first (Mishnah Oholot 7:6).
Church of England: lesser of two evils in strictly limited cases.
Saving one life is better than losing both; compassion (Matthew 5:7).
Evaluation: strong because it upholds the sanctity of the mother's life.
against: Catholic: direct abortion always wrong; life protected from conception (CCC 2270).
Both lives are equally sacred; doctors should try to save both.
Ending an innocent life is still killing (Exodus 20:13).
But double effect allows life-saving treatment.
Evaluation: principled, but reaches a similar result in practice.
exam.conclusion: Nearly all traditions allow the mother's life to be saved even if the foetus dies; they differ only on whether its death may be directly intended, so believers should accept this.

short.a: Hospice care (accept: palliative care; pain relief).

short.q: Give one religious reason against euthanasia.
short.a: Only God should end life (accept: sanctity of life; 'You shall not murder'; Ecclesiastes 3:2; suffering can have meaning).

short.q: Name one type of euthanasia.
short.a: Voluntary (accept: non-voluntary, involuntary, active, passive).

short.q: Give one Christian belief about life after death.
short.a: Resurrection (accept: judgement, heaven, hell, purgatory, eternal life).

short.q: Give one non-religious argument against life after death.
short.a: There is no scientific evidence (accept: the mind depends on the brain; wishful thinking).

short.q: Name the Jewish belief in the world to come.
short.a: Olam Ha-Ba.
